title: Violin
summary: Not yet indistinguishable from a real violin. Pressure comes from a compact receiver and the body's modes stop at 5 kHz. E5 is too dark, A4 and B4 sound cleaner than the recording, B6 sounds 26 cents flat (the note sits on the lower of two branches that meet near the string's third, read from four probe stations), and the stopped notes B4 and B6 score below every open note. Four Dominant strings (Pickering's sections), each with two polarisations, drive a computed shell of the Guarneri il Cannone's scanned geometry in spruce and maple, with its enclosed air through an f-hole neck. The bow grips through the friction law measured on real rosin. G3, B3, B4, D4, A4 and E5 use a bow of finite width with hair compliance. G3 also carries the air load on the shell's outside (the skin). Stopped notes press a fingertip on the string with 3.5 N; of them B3 and B4 carry a finite-width bow, and all four carry the strings' residual flexibility. The open strings are tuned to equal temperament, never to a recording.
physics_present: four strings from compiled Dominant section packs (Pickering 1985), each with two transverse polarisations; all four stay coupled through the bridge while one is bowed

a computed shell body from il Cannone's scanned geometry (Guarneri 1743) with the corrected f-hole shape: Norway spruce (Viala 2020) for the top, bass bar and soundpost, sycamore maple (Sonderegger 2013) for the back, ribs and bridge, 134 modes on the 6 mm mesh
the enclosed air as one cavity through a physical f-hole neck, its conductance from a boundary-element computation of the f-holes

on G3, at 192 kHz: the air load on the shell's outside from a boundary-element computation (the body-radiation skin), with the f-hole neck's outer end handed to it. It changes how the body moves, not how the note is picked up. With it alone the air mode's Q is 52, against 19 printed (Jansson) and 19 without it. Nothing is dropped: the skin radiates into full space, which is right for a body this small against the wavelength, where the older compact neck end radiated into a half-space and so matched the print for the wrong reason. The viscous loss at the edge of each measured f-hole is now added on G3, each hole the circle of its own area with its own wall thickness (5.31 cm2 and 2.51 mm, 4.98 cm2 and 2.28 mm) and the air flow split between them by conductance: it takes the air mode's Q to 30 at 275.6 Hz, where the row was predicted to put it, and the rest of the gap to the printed 19 is unexplained. A control on that render's binary, the live G3 card without the hole row, reproduces the live clip byte for byte, so the change is the row's alone
the steady-sliding friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025, eq. 13) on every note
a bow of finite width (10 mm in 3 cells) with hair compliance after Pitteroff and Woodhouse 1998, on G3, B3, B4, D4, A4 and E5
the exact static compliance of each string's omitted modes at its bridge (residual flexibility), on the open notes G3, D4, A4 and E5, and on the stopped B3, B4, B5 and B6
a rigid fingertip pressed onto the string with 3.5 N (Issanchou et al. 2017 contact law), held by a static preload, on the stopped notes B3, B4, B5 and B6
longitudinal string waves and thermochemical room air (N2, O2, Ar, CO2) on A4; dry air (N2 0.8, O2 0.2) as one gas state on the other notes
open strings tuned to equal temperament (A4 = 440 Hz) by a tension factor read from the assembled instrument's own pulse response, never from a recording
physics_missing: a radiating exterior: pressure on every page is the shell's volume and the cavity at 1 m through a compact receiver, with no directivity and no finite receiver. A directional receiver at the recording's microphone point (the one_way_observer row) was tried on G3 and refused before any sound: the shell's own triangles, which are its radiating skin, resolve six panels per wavelength only up to 2773 Hz, so a receiver that carries the whole page needs a finer CT shell mesh than the 6 mm one, and the CT data have none finer.

enough sound for the plates' motion: between about 1250 and 2000 Hz the plates move about as much per newton as Bissinger's print, within 4 dB, but give 3 to 8 dB too little sound on a finite receiver and 10 to 13 dB on the compact receiver the pages use; his two sets reach the critical line at about 3.5 and 4.3 kHz, and ours doesn't by 4 kHz
body modes above 5 kHz, and any mesh convergence: every page is on the 6 mm mesh's 134 modes
air modes beyond the one cavity
the strings' tension loss: no printed loss exists for these strings
the string-to-bridge joint's contact mechanics: an authored spring and dashpot per string (200000 N/m, 0.1 N s/m)

the finite-width bow and hair compliance on the stopped notes B5 and B6. B6 was tried with the hair rows. Inside the graded first 0.7 s it rose from 7 to 8 of 15 and moved 21 c up, to -4.7 c of ET (gap to the recording 52.9 -> 31.5 c). After 0.7 s, with the bow still drawn at the card's force and speed, its level fell 20 dB under the posted page and its fundamental 22.7 dB, so H2 stands level with H1. The recording cannot show how a longer stroke behaves: its note ends near 0.6 s, and the recording is silent from 1.71 s after its onset. So B6 keeps its page. A traced 1.2 s probe of that card shows each of the 10 mm ribbon's three cells in Helmholtz motion, one fast slip per period. Between those slips the bridge-side and centre cells slip slowly about three more times per period and the far cell once. Each cell carries a third of the 0.159 N bow force. The bow is a 10 mm hair ribbon of three contact cells. On the same B6 card with the E string at 28 modes, five cells keep one fast slip per period on every cell and hold the pitch within 2 c and the level within 1 dB of three cells over 0.15-0.25 s, but harmonics 2 to 8 stand 2 to 3 dB higher against the fundamental; seven cells stop at 0.088 s (sample 12664), where the friction solver misses the one consistent contact state. So three cells is not yet shown to be converged. B5 was tried with the hair rows on its posted card and keeps its page: it renders the full 3 s without a clip, but comes out much cleaner than the recording, harmonics-to-noise 47.7 dB against 14.0 dB (19.9 dB on the page), and falls from 8 to 7 of 15.

friction beyond steady sliding: no rosin temperature and no friction memory. The thermal rosin row (Smith and Woodhouse 2000, as printed) stays off. On the bare metal string, its one-dimensional heat flow into the stationary surface, which the paper excuses only where that surface conducts little heat, holds the contact near ambient for seconds, so the bow slides at near-static friction and the note speaks late. On the rosin-shielded string that Woodhouse (2003) prints, the contact heats past the end of the measured friction curve within 0.15 s, where the row stops. Run past the 5 m/s its authors print the curve to (their extrapolated fit, not a measurement; Smith and Woodhouse keep their own runs below 40 K above ambient, "probably low enough for plausibility of this model"), D4 plays its whole stroke in Helmholtz motion: the contact passes 39.06 K above ambient only in the slip pulses, on 15 % of the sliding samples, peaking at 42.5 K, and the note comes out far cleaner than the recording (harmonics-to-noise 69 dB against 28), falling from 14 to 8 of 14.

the fingertip's own loss and contact width: the finger is a rigid point stop; printed fingertip pads (Wiertlewski and Hayward 2012) are measured on a flat plate up to 500 Hz, and no contact width on a string is printed
string modes above about 9.6 kHz on the E string, which carries 17 sines, so B6's 5th harmonic has no string mode under it
a player: constant bow speed and force, where the real E5 keeps swelling for about a second after it speaks
one co-characterised instrument: il Cannone's geometry is combined with independently sourced wood and string data
